\chapter{You, Singular and Plural}
\label{ch:la-you-singular-plural}

\section[tū / vōs]{tū, vōs — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} before politeness got involved}

\label{lesson:LA-C22-tu-vos}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} German's lesson on \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} was about \textbf{formality} — \emph{du} versus \emph{Sie}. Latin's version of this same lesson is about something completely different: plain \textbf{number}. Formality hadn't been invented yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tū — you, one person}
\textbf{Tū} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you},\textquotedblright{} addressing \textbf{one} person. That's the whole rule — no formal/informal split, just singular number. You've already used its dative form, \emph{tibi}, in \emph{quid tibi nōmen est?}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vōs — you, more than one person}
\textbf{Vōs} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you},\textquotedblright{} addressing \textbf{more than one} person — plain plural, nothing more.

\begin{culture}
Here's the real teaching point: in \textbf{Classical Latin}, this is a \textbf{purely grammatical number} distinction. There is \textbf{no} formal/informal dimension at all — using \emph{vōs} to politely address a single powerful person had \textbf{not yet started}. That habit — plural pronoun used respectfully for one person — only developed later, in \textbf{Late Latin}, well after the classical period. It's the \textbf{direct ancestor} of French's polite \emph{vous}. Careful, though: it is \textbf{not} the ancestor of German's \emph{Sie} from the last lesson — \emph{Sie} solves the same politeness problem in a completely \textbf{different} way, by repurposing an unrelated pronoun (3rd-person plural \textquotedblleft{}they\textquotedblright{}), not by descending from \emph{vōs} at all. Classical Romans simply didn't have this option yet: one person was always \emph{tū}, no matter how important they were — though Romans still had \textbf{other} ways to show deference, like respectful titles (\emph{domine}, \textquotedblleft{}sir/lord\textquotedblright{}), just not through the pronoun itself.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}tū\textquotedblright{} — you, singular, one person{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}vōs\textquotedblright{} — you, plural, more than one person{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest twist — Classical Latin's tū/vōs is PURE number, no politeness at all, unlike German's du/Sie{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What's the difference between \textbf{tū} and \textbf{vōs} in Classical Latin — number, or politeness? (\textbf{Pure number} — \emph{tū} is singular, \emph{vōs} is plural; no formality dimension existed yet.) When did using \emph{vōs} to politely address one person begin? (\textbf{Late Latin}, after the classical period — the direct ancestor of French's polite \emph{vous}.) Is German's \textbf{Sie} descended from \emph{vōs} the same way? (\textbf{No} — \emph{Sie} solves the same problem independently, by repurposing 3rd-person plural \textquotedblleft{}they,\textquotedblright{} not by inheriting from \emph{vōs} at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
